Dynamic tariff offerings will likely offer many more complexities than what is modeled here; fixed charges, subscriptions, asymmetric buy/sell prices, and other rate design features will change what is possible in terms of the hourly price, what is optimal for customer load response, and what is cost effective for automation technology. 56 Additionally, principles of rate design may require that dynamic prices be set such that they, as accurately as possible, mimic the true cost of providing the electricity in each hour. In theory, the marginal avoided costs analyzed in this study represent a reasonable proxy for this cost basis. As shown in Figure 23, the Mild tariff drives bill savings that most closely mimic the scale of avoided costs estimated. This means that the more “aggressive” dynamic prices shown in the Medium and Full scenarios, while beneficial for motivating load response and providing significant customer bill savings, may not align well with hourly costs and may ultimately overcompensate price responsive behaviors. Of course, many programs start out by intentionally incentivizing desired behaviors beyond true costs (e.g. NEM rates for PV), in order to develop technologies and customer acceptance, and therefore more attractive dynamic price designs may be considered for this purpose. 4.3 Customer participation in dynamic pricing The flexibility potentials shown in this study reflect a world with universal enrollment in dynamic tariffs, widespread adoption of automation technologies, and complete enablement of such technologies to shift the end use loads. This scenario is far from expected; even when the payback period for load flexibility technologies is short and the financial savings of price response are clear, several additional factors will impact customers’ choice to not only adopt such enabling technologies, but to select a dynamic price as their electricity tariff to begin with. Several factors contribute to the decision-making process when considering dynamic tariffs and enabling price responsiveness. Customers’ likelihood of switching to a dynamic tariff will depend not only on their potential bill impacts, but their overall willingness to engage with new price structures. Many customers may see dynamic tariffs as being very complex, feeling the need to track fluctuating prices on a day- by-day basis and adjust their behavior accordingly. Even with potential savings on the table, the perceived effort required to navigate this structure can outweigh the perceived benefits, especially for those who prefer simplicity in their billing. Further, there may be significant real and/or perceived risk associated with selecting a dynamic tariff. Customers may worry about price spikes during high-demand periods leading to unexpectedly large bills. While these high price periods are evened out by ample low-price hours, the fear of unpredictably high bills may deter customers. These concerns can be mitigated by safeguards like price caps or bill protection programs, and by customer education that emphasizes the opportunity that dynamic pricing creates to access low-cost electricity.
